tagline.text: Boracay's wind-swept eastern beach for kitesurfing and windsurfing

location.label: Location
location.text: East coast of Boracay Island, Malay, Aklan (across from White Beach)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–April Amihan (northeast wind) season, with the steadiest wind from December to March

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half a day to a full day

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–10,000 (browsing and meals are cheap; a 3-hour kite lesson costs about ₱7,000–10,000, per person)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Kalibo International Airport (KLO) or Caticlan Airport (MPH), then by boat

children.text: Bulabog Beach is the hub for kitesurfing and windsurfing on the east side of Boracay, directly across from White Beach. In the shallow, reef-protected lagoon you ride the Amihan wind from November to April, and in the windless wet season it becomes a quiet strip of cafes and guesthouses.

Bulabog Beach lies on the east coast of Boracay Island. It faces White Beach on the west across the island's narrow waist, so if White Beach is the sandy stage for sunsets, this side is the windy water-sports beach. Wikipedia describes it as the second most popular tourist beach on the island. Maps place it a little differently, at roughly 11.964–11.969°N and 121.927–121.931°E. One source gives the beach a length of about
2.5km
, so the coordinates shift slightly depending on which point is used.

The reason it became a famous windsurfing and kitesurfing spot is the wind. According to Wikipedia, during the dry Amihan season (roughly October to March) the wind blows from the east, and hills at the island's northern and southern ends funnel it toward Bulabog. A reef encircles the water off the beach, so it is relatively shallow and safe. A kite-specialist site explains that the shallow lagoon is smooth at low tide and turns into "bump 'n' jump" conditions at high tide, and also says these conditions suit learners. It is also known as the venue of the Boracay International Funboard Cup, a week-long competition usually held each January.

Unlike White Beach, the sand here is not powdery, and there are patches of coral and seagrass. It draws people who come to ride the wind rather than people who mainly want to swim. Along the beach are kite and windsurf schools, gear rental, cafes and guesthouses, and with coconut trees lining the shore the mood is relaxed. Access is free, and you only pay for lessons and food at the individual businesses. When the wind drops in the wet season, the sea calms and there are many days that are good for swimming.

Boracay was closed for six months for rehabilitation from April 26, 2018 and reopened on October 26. Explanations mention new rules such as a 30-meter setback from the waterline, but I could not confirm how they apply to Bulabog specifically. Prices and rules in this guide are approximate, based on recent public sources, so check with schools, lodging or the tourism office before you go.

This is Boracay's flagship kite spot. The lagoon inside the reef is shallow, and several schools line the beach, offering everything from beginner lessons to free-use rentals for experienced riders. Experienced riders are said to ride a small reef break beyond the reef.

Windsurf centers share the beach with the kite schools. The Boracay International Funboard Cup, held for a week each January, is known as this beach's signature event. The schedule differs each year, so check.
The steadiest wind comes from December to March, typically 15–25 knots and occasionally above 30 according to one source. November and April are the shoulder months on either side.

blocks.title: A calm sea in the wet season

children.text: In the June–October Habagat season the wind shifts west, so kite sessions at Bulabog become irregular or impossible on many days. On such days, however, the sea is calm, and one source says the beach serves as a jumping-off point for other water activities.
Casual cafes and guesthouses line the beach, and unlike White Beach there are few daybed clubs, so it is described as relatively quiet even at midday.

blocks.title: Swimming and snorkeling area in the lagoon

children.text: One source says a marked swimming and snorkeling area lies toward the south. Check the area's location and whether lifeguards are present once you arrive.
Because the island is narrow, you can reportedly walk from White Beach. One source says it takes about 10–15 minutes from around Station 2, but ask locally about the exact route.

Kite lesson prices vary widely by school. One guide site lists a 3-hour introductory lesson at ₱10,000 and a 1-hour taster at ₱5,500, while another lists about ₱7,000 for 3 hours and around ₱3,500 for a day of gear rental.

items.title: Half-day visit and trial
items.subtitle: Crossing over from White Beach as part of a day plan

children.text: Have breakfast at your lodging near White Beach, then head to Bulabog. Because the island is narrow, you can walk or take a tricycle. One source says it takes about
10–15 minutes
Have coffee at a beachside cafe and see how strongly the wind is blowing. In the Amihan season you can watch kites fill the sky.
If you have booked a kite trial or windsurfing, listen to the school's briefing. Beginners usually first spend about
1.5–2 hours
with a small kite learning kite control and safety.
Have lunch at a beachfront restaurant and rest. When the wind is strong around midday, lessons at the kite schools carry on, so watching them is a good way to spend the time.
If there is a swimming area, enter the water at a calm time. Returning to White Beach before sunset to watch it is also a good plan.
The wind varies from day to day, so leave room in your schedule and book lessons for more than one day in a row.
Take lessons on kite control and safety. Practice with a small kite.
Practice body dragging, being pulled through the water by the kite. One source says many students are ready to ride around the third lesson.
Try riding with the board. According to one source, riders can ride in light wind after about 9–12 hours of lessons.

items.title: From Manila by air and boat

children.text: Fly from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) to Kalibo (KLO) or Caticlan (MPH). Caticlan Airport is the closest to Boracay, and from Kalibo you take a bus or van to Caticlan jetty port. Check airline notices for routes and timetables.

From Caticlan jetty port you cross to Boracay by pump boat or speedboat. One source lists ₱25 (regular) or ₱150 (chartered) for the trip from the port to Bulabog, but this is past information, so confirm locally.
Environmental fees and terminal charges may apply separately when you enter Boracay, so check the latest rules.

items.title: On foot or by tricycle from White Beach

children.text: Because the island is narrow, one description says it takes about
10–15 minutes
on foot from around Station 2 of White Beach to Bulabog.
You can also go by tricycle or electric tricycle. The fare depends on distance and passengers, so agree on it before you ride.
Some lesson packages say they include pickup from hotels at Stations 1–3 to the school. Check the pickup time slot when you book.

Bulabog is a seasonal beach. The best time for kiting and windsurfing is the Amihan season from November to April, and many sources say the wind is steadiest from December to March. This also overlaps with peak tourist season, so Boracay is crowded from the year's end through February.

From June to October the wind shifts west and Bulabog's wind becomes weak or irregular. Kiting is hard to expect then, but calm mornings are actually good for swimming, and lodging prices drop. Rain and typhoons are more likely, so check the weather forecast.

Seasonal boundaries differ slightly between sources. Wikipedia gives Amihan as roughly October to March, kite guide sites say November to April, and some even list May and October as good months. So if you really want to kite, plan for December to March, and bear in mind that the wind may not blow in other months.

Bulabog has guesthouses, small hotels and rooms attached to kite schools. For those who come to ride the wind, staying close to a school is convenient, and one description says White Beach is within walking distance. In peak season book early, and in the wet season rates drop considerably. Specific businesses change over time, so choose based on recent reviews.

Meals are handled by cafes and restaurants along the beach. One description says the cafes are relatively quiet by day, and menus and prices differ by shop. The restaurants of White Beach are within walking distance, so you can also head there for dinner.

Here are some pointers for first-time visitors to Bulabog. If you want to learn kiting, set your lesson dates first and then choose lodging. If you only want to watch, base yourself near White Beach and cross over for half a day. On days with weak wind a school may propose changing the schedule, so ask about refund and change policies in advance.
Wear aqua shoes when swimming, because there are sea urchins and pieces of coral on the seabed.
For kite lessons, choose an IKO-certified instructor and small class sizes. Check the price and what is included beforehand.
Around midday the wind is strong and the sun and blown sand are harsh, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
You can rent or store gear at the schools. Leave valuables at your lodging or school.
The best times for swimming are windless mornings or the wet season. Act as if there are no lifeguards.
Check wind forecasts with an app such as Windfinder, and book lessons with some extra days to spare.
If there is no trash bin at the beach, take your trash with you.
Schools and lodging fill up early in peak season, so book ahead.
On windy days kites, boards and debris come close to the beach. Swim and play only in designated areas, and keep away from kite lines.
There are sea urchins and sharp coral, stones and shells, so wear shoes when entering and leaving the water.
In the Habagat season the wind is irregular and plans may be canceled.
Do not assume that lifeguards are present.
Guard against pickpocketing and loss by leaving valuables at your lodging.
Prices and rules differ by school and season, so always check.
A guide to the whole island. White Beach, sunsets and the dining areas are within walking distance.
A shell-strewn beach in the north of Boracay. You can get there by tricycle or motorcycle, and travel time depends on traffic.
One of the gateway cities to Boracay, from where you travel overland from the airport to Caticlan jetty port.
The island's signature beach on the west side. It is covered in the Boracay entry here, and is described as within walking distance of Bulabog.
